screens.title: Functions, Visibility, and State Variables
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we will build a clear mental model of Solidity functions, why visibility matters, and how state lives on-chain. Functions are the units of behavior in a smart contract: they accept inputs, produce outputs, and may read or change persistent state. Visibility specifiers — public, private, internal, external — control who can call those functions and are a primary security boundary. State mutability specifiers — view, pure, payable, or none — describe whether a function reads state, only computes, or can accept Ether. State variables, declared outside functions, are stored permanently on the blockchain and are costly to change. Throughout the chapter you'll see concrete code examples, a hands-on SimpleWallet activity, and common mistakes to avoid, like exposing sensitive functions or forgetting payable. By the end you will be able to choose the correct visibility and mutability for a function, manage state variables safely, and implement a basic owner-only access control using msg. sender and require. Notice practical trade-offs: tighter visibility reduces attack surface; pure and view can be called off-chain for free. Keep these ideas in mind as we walk through examples and a live-demo style walkthrough.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will meet four measurable objectives. First, you will be able to define and declare functions in Solidity, including parameters and return values. That means writing correct signatures and returning values where appropriate, and understanding how parameters map to memory locations. Second, you will understand and correctly apply function visibility: public, private, internal, and external, and why choosing the most restrictive visibility reduces attack surface. Third, you will differentiate view, pure, and payable functions, knowing which are free when called off-chain and which accept Ether, and how they affect gas usage. Fourth, you will manage state variables and implement a basic access control mechanism using msg. sender and require so only an owner can run sensitive functions. Each objective includes a short practice milestone: write a utility pure function; convert a setter to external for gas efficiency where appropriate; add payable to a deposit handler; and implement owner-only withdraw logic. These objectives are practical and testable in Remix. Work through the provided SimpleWallet activity to verify each milestone and reflect on a scenario where external is more gas-efficient than public.

screens.title: Bloom Progression
screens.narratorSegment: This mini-bar guides how you'll move from comprehension to mastery. Learn means you can name and write basic function signatures and state variables. Understand means you can explain the differences between public, private, internal, and external, and state mutability choices. Apply means you will actually implement access control in a contract, mark functions view or pure when appropriate, and test deposit and withdraw behavior in Remix. Master involves choosing the most restrictive visibility by default, minimizing state writes to reduce gas, and reasoning about when external is preferable for array parameters because of calldata efficiency. screens.title: What is a function in Solidity?
screens.narratorSegment: A function in Solidity is a named block of code that performs a task, accepts parameters, and can return values. Unlike functions in off-chain languages, Solidity functions also carry metadata: visibility and state mutability specifiers that affect access and gas. When you declare a function you specify its signature — name, parameter types, and return types — and then choose visibility and mutability. For example, a function that only computes and returns a value should be marked pure; one that reads state but doesn't modify it should be view. A function intended to receive Ether must be marked payable. A practical example is a calculateTax function that takes an amount and returns ten percent; it doesn't touch state and should be declared pure so callers can run it off-chain for free. A common misconception is thinking that view or pure always cost no gas; they are free when executed off-chain, but if they are called from another contract in a transaction they still consume gas. Key takeaway: choose the right signature and specifiers to make your intent explicit and your contract safer and cheaper to interact with. Ask yourself: does this function need to modify state or receive Ether? If not, mark it view or pure.

keyIdea.title: Function basics
keyIdea.text: Declare a clear signature and use mutability to indicate read/write behavior and whether Ether may be received.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › What is a function?
Definition

A function encapsulates a task and its inputs/outputs, plus visibility and mutability that govern access and state effects.

Concrete example
function calculateTax(uint amount) public pure returns (uint) {
    return amount / 10; // 10% tax
}
This function is pure because it only computes from its input and doesn't read or modify contract state.
Misconception
view or pure always free — clarify: they are free off-chain, but cost gas when called within on-chain transactions.
Key Takeaway
Mark intent with mutability to communicate behavior and optimize gas when possible.
Anatomy of a function
  • Signature: name and parameter types control how callers pass data.
  • Returns: specify return types so callers can use outputs directly.
  • Visibility: who can call this function externally or internally.
  • Mutability: whether it reads, writes, or receives Ether.
Check your understanding
Write a function that computes square of an input without reading state and mark it with the correct specifier.

screens.title: Visibility specifiers explained
screens.narratorSegment: Visibility specifiers control where a function can be called from and are a critical access control layer. Public functions are callable from anywhere: externally, internally, and through inheritance. Private functions are callable only inside the defining contract and cannot be accessed by derived contracts. Internal functions are callable within the contract and by derived contracts, but not by external accounts. External functions can be called from outside the contract; they are often more gas-efficient for large calldata parameters because arguments are read directly from calldata instead of being copied to memory. A concrete example from the source shows a public getter that returns a state value and an external setter that updates it then calls an internal helper. A common pitfall is making administrative logic public by accident; default to the most restrictive visibility and widen only when needed. Another trap is thinking external functions cannot be called internally — they can be, but with different semantics and potential gas implications. Key takeaway: pick the narrowest visibility that still supports your required interactions, and test callability in Remix to validate your assumptions.

keyIdea.title: Visibility rule
keyIdea.text: Use the narrowest visibility appropriate: private/internal for helpers; external/public for external APIs, with external preferred for large calldata inputs.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Visibility specifiers
Quick comparison
public
Callable externally and internally. Good for getters and public APIs.
external
Callable only from outside. More gas-efficient for large calldata arrays.
internal
Callable within contract and by derived contracts. Use for shared behavior in inheritance.
private
Callable only in the defining contract. Use for sensitive helpers not meant for inheritance.
Example snippet
uint public data;

function setDataExternal(uint _newData) external {
  data = _newData;
  _internalUpdate();
}

function _internalUpdate() internal { data += 1; }
Explanation cards
  • External is suited for large arrays because calldata avoids an extra memory copy.
  • Internal/private functions are preferred for helper logic to reduce exposed attack surface.
  • Public getters are convenient, but avoid exposing mutating admin functions publicly.
Common mistake
Marking sensitive state-changing functions public by default instead of restricting them with internal or private and access checks.
Key Takeaway
Default to the most restrictive visibility that still allows necessary interactions; only widen visibility intentionally.

screens.title: State mutability specifiers
screens.narratorSegment: State mutability specifiers tell readers and the EVM how a function interacts with blockchain state and Ether. A view function promises not to modify state; it may read state variables and is free when called off-chain. A pure function promises not to read or modify state; it only computes using its inputs and local variables. Payable functions are the only ones that can receive Ether; forgetting to mark a deposit handler payable will revert incoming transfers. Functions with no mutability specifier can both read and write state and will always cost gas when executed on-chain. Consider the deposit and getBalance examples: deposit must be payable to accept msg. value and update balances; getBalance should be view to allow off-chain reads without gas. A common misconception is assuming payable forces a function to process Ether; it only allows Ether to be sent. You still need to inspect msg. value and update state or revert as your logic requires. Key takeaway: choose view/pure to signal and enable free off-chain reads, and use payable only when your function intentionally accepts Ether. State mutability specifiers means mark read-only functions view or pure to reduce cost for callers; mark deposit handlers payable and check msg.value when accepting ether.. In practical terms, view, pure, payable and when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Mark read-only functions view or pure to reduce cost for callers; mark deposit handlers payable and check msg.value when accepting Ether.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › State mutability
Mutability types
view
Reads state but does not modify it. Free off-chain.
pure
Does not read or modify state. Pure computations only.
payable
Allows the function to receive Ether via msg.value.
Example: deposit
function deposit() public payable {
  balance += msg.value;
}
Deposit must be payable to accept Ether. msg.value contains the amount sent.
Best practices & pitfalls
  • Mark view and pure whenever possible to document intent and enable free off-chain inspection.
  • Only use payable when a function must accept Ether; otherwise revert accidental transfers by omitting payable.
  • Remember: view and pure are only free when called off-chain; on-chain calls still consume gas.
Key Takeaway
Use mutability specifiers to communicate behavior, prevent accidental Ether acceptance, and reduce cost for readers.

screens.title: State variables and storage
screens.narratorSegment: State variables are declared outside functions and persist in the contract's storage on the blockchain. They are the contract's canonical data and modifying them is the most expensive operation in terms of gas. In practice you should minimize writes, batch updates when possible, and avoid unnecessary writes inside loops. For example, the SimpleWallet contract defines state variables owner and balance; the constructor sets owner using msg. sender and balance is updated in deposit and withdraw functions. Accessing a state variable from a function is straightforward, but remember that reading from storage is cheaper than writing but still costs gas when done within a transaction. A common error is redundantly storing data that can be derived or computed, which inflates gas costs and storage usage. Also be aware of shadowing variables in derived contracts — internal visibility allows inheritance but requires careful naming to avoid accidental overrides. Key takeaway: treat state writes as intentional and costly; design your functions to minimize writes and to validate conditions before changing state, using require to avoid wasted gas on failing operations. State variables and storage means declare persistent data outside functions; minimize writes and validate before modifying storage to avoid wasted gas.. In practical terms, how variables declared outside functions persist on-chain. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: State variables
keyIdea.text: Declare persistent data outside functions; minimize writes and validate before modifying storage to avoid wasted gas.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › State variables
Persistent storage

Variables declared at contract scope are stored on-chain. Reads and writes interact with storage and affect gas differently: reads cost less than writes, writes are the most expensive.

Example from SimpleWallet
address public owner;
uint public balance;

constructor() { owner = msg.sender; balance = 0; }
Owner is set at deployment using msg.sender. Balance is tracked explicitly, though address(this).balance also reflects Ether stored in the contract.
Common mistake
Unnecessary state writes inside loops or failing to validate conditions before updating state, which wastes gas and can break transactions.
Pro tip
Compute values off-chain or use view/pure for reads. Batch state updates when possible and validate early with require to avoid wasted gas.
Why it matters
Storage is permanent and paid for. Efficient state management makes your contract cheaper to use and more secure by reducing attack surface where state is changed.
Key Takeaway
Design state writes intentionally and validate inputs before changing storage to save gas and avoid errors.

screens.title: SimpleWallet starter review
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the SimpleWallet starter contract to see these ideas in action. The constructor sets owner to msg. sender at deployment and initializes balance. The deposit function is public and payable; it increments the internal balance by msg. value so the contract tracks deposits explicitly. The getContractBalance function is declared view and returns address(this). balance; this is a read-only operation safe for off-chain calls. The withdraw function is intentionally left with TODOs: it must check that msg. sender equals owner, verify the contract has sufficient balance, perform the transfer, and update the internal balance. When implementing withdraw you should call require(msg. sender == owner, "Only owner can withdraw.") and require(address(this). balance >= _amount, "Insufficient balance.") before transferring funds. A typical mistake is transferring Ether before updating state or failing to guard with require, which can enable unauthorized withdrawals or reentrancy. The guided activity asks you to implement withdraw and test it using different Remix accounts so you observe reverts and successful transfers. Reflect: why should we prefer updating state before external calls to avoid reentrancy? SimpleWallet starter review means complete withdraw with require checks, verify balances, transfer safely, and update internal tracking to avoid vulnerabilities.. In practical terms, constructor, deposit, view getter, and withdraw todos. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › SimpleWallet walkthrough
Starter code (annotated)
contract SimpleWallet {
    address public owner;
    uint public balance;

    constructor() {
        owner = msg.sender;
        balance = 0;
    }

    function deposit() public payable {
        balance += msg.value;
    }

    function getContractBalance() public view returns (uint) {
        return address(this).balance;
    }

    function withdraw(uint _amount) public {
        // TODO: Implement access control and safe transfer
    }
}
This code demonstrates constructor initialization, a payable deposit handler, and a view getter that returns the contract's Ether balance. Your task is to implement withdraw robustly using require checks and safe sequencing of state updates and transfers.
Example checklist
  • Add require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can withdraw.").
  • Ensure address(this).balance >= _amount before transfer.
  • Perform state update before external calls to reduce reentrancy risk.
Common mistake
Transferring Ether and then updating internal balance; this can leave state inconsistent if the transfer fails or reentrancy occurs.
Key Takeaway
Require checks first, update state before external calls, and test from multiple accounts to validate access control.

screens.title: Implementing access control with require and msg.sender
screens.narratorSegment: Access control is succinctly implemented using msg. sender and require. Msg. sender holds the address initiating the external call. A common owner-only pattern stores owner in a state variable at construction and then checks caller identity with require(msg. sender == owner, "Only owner can...");. The process is straightforward: first, declare owner as a state variable and set it in the constructor using msg. sender. Second, write the sensitive function and at the top enforce the require check. Third, verify preconditions like available balance with another require. Fourth, perform state updates, and finally perform external transfers if needed. For example, in withdraw you check ownership, check sufficient funds, subtract the internal balance tracking, and then transfer Ether. A misconception is trusting msg. sender when using delegatecall or proxy patterns; in simple contracts msg. sender is reliable for owner checks, but proxies change the caller context. Always test access control by trying to call privileged functions from a non-owner account and observing the revert. Key takeaway: enforce checks early, validate state, update storage, and then interact with external addresses. Implementing access control with require and msg.sender means store owner on deployment, require msg.sender equality in sensitive functions, validate state, update storage, then perform external transfers.. In practical terms, a step-by-step pattern for owner-only functions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

In practical terms, a step-by-step pattern for owner-only functions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. keyIdea.title: Access control pattern
keyIdea.text: Store owner on deployment, require msg.sender equality in sensitive functions, validate state, update storage, then perform external transfers.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Access control process
Step-by-step
  1. Set owner in constructor: owner = msg.sender.
  2. At function start, check require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can ...").
  3. Validate preconditions, e.g., sufficient balance.
  4. Update state to reflect the change before external calls.
  5. Execute safe transfer to the owner.
Concrete example
function withdraw(uint _amount) public {
    require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can withdraw.");
    require(address(this).balance >= _amount, "Insufficient balance.");
    balance -= _amount;
    payable(msg.sender).transfer(_amount);
}
Warnings & checks
  • Update state before transfer to reduce reentrancy exposure.
  • Ensure require messages are descriptive to ease debugging.
  • Test from non-owner accounts to confirm reverts and from owner to confirm success.
Key Takeaway
Use msg.sender checks with require to gate sensitive functions and validate state before making changes or sending Ether.

screens.title: view vs pure vs payable vs state-changing
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the contrast between view, pure, payable, and normal state-changing functions helps you design efficient and correct contracts. View functions read state but do not modify it; they allow off-chain callers to fetch data without submitting a transaction. Pure functions do not read or modify state and are ideal for utility calculations; both view and pure are free to call off-chain. Payable functions are allowed to receive Ether and must explicitly be marked so, otherwise incoming Ether will cause a revert. Functions without any mutability specifier can change state and therefore always cost gas when executed on-chain. A concrete example: getContractBalance is view and returns address(this). balance; calculateSum is pure and simply returns a sum; deposit is payable and updates state. A common contrast to check is that view and pure do not guarantee zero gas when they are invoked from on-chain context — they still cost gas when called from other contracts. Key takeaway: use the most restrictive mutability that fits the function's purpose and remember to mark deposit handlers payable when they must accept Ether. view vs pure vs payable vs state-changing means choose pure for pure computation, view for read-only state access, payable to accept ether, and no specifier for functions that modify storage.. In practical terms, read-only, compute-only, ether receivers, and mutating functions contrasted. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Choose pure for pure computation, view for read-only state access, payable to accept Ether, and no specifier for functions that modify storage.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Mutability comparison
Examples
pure: calculateSum(uint a,uint b) public pure returns (uint)
view: getContractBalance() public view returns (uint)
payable: deposit() public payable { balance += msg.value; }
state-changing: increment() public { counter++; }
Practical notes
  • Prefer pure for deterministic utilities and view for read-only queries.
  • Mark deposit handlers payable and inspect msg.value to confirm expected transfers.
  • Remember off-chain calls to view/pure are free; on-chain calls still cost gas.
Key Takeaway
Pick the narrowest mutability that reflects the function's behavior to communicate intent and enable cost savings for off-chain inspection.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › SimpleWallet lab
Lab checklist
  1. Create SimpleWallet.sol and paste the starter code.
  2. Compile and deploy to JavaScript VM; record owner address.
  3. From a different account, call deposit and send Ether.
  4. Confirm getContractBalance and balance reflect the deposit.
  5. Implement withdraw with require checks, update balance, and transfer Ether.
  6. Test withdraw from owner (should succeed) and non-owner (should revert).
Reflection prompt
Why is updating internal state before making external transfers a safer pattern? Consider reentrancy and failure handling.
Hints
  • Use require with clear error messages for easier debugging.
  • Test deposit and withdraw with small Ether amounts first in the JavaScript VM.
  • Remember that msg.sender is the caller and msg.value is the Ether sent.
Key Takeaway
Walk through the entire deposit-to-withdraw flow and test both success and failure cases to validate access control and state updates.

screens.title: Pitfalls and safety notes
screens.narratorSegment: This screen highlights common mistakes you should avoid. First, incorrect visibility: exposing sensitive functions as public instead of private or internal can allow unauthorized actors to change state or drain funds. Second, missing payable: forgetting to mark a deposit handler payable causes incoming Ether to revert, leading to failed transactions and poor UX. Third, unchecked msg. sender: failing to validate caller identity for privileged operations allows unauthorized access; use require(msg. sender == owner, "...") to enforce ownership. Fourth, gas costs of state changes: writes to storage are expensive; design functions to minimize state writes and avoid unnecessary storage updates inside loops. Finally, reentrancy: never transfer Ether and then update state — update state first, then transfer, and consider using checks-effects-interactions pattern. A misconception to clear up is that view and pure always save gas; they are free only off-chain. When called in a transaction from another contract, they still cost gas. The takeaway is to be explicit: choose the most restrictive visibility, mark functions payable only when needed, validate msg. sender, and minimize writes to control gas and attack surface.

keyIdea.title: Safety checklist
keyIdea.text: Avoid exposing admin functions, mark payable intentionally, validate callers with require, and minimize state writes to control gas and risks.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Pitfalls & safety
Top mistakes
  • Leaving critical functions public when they should be restricted.
  • Not marking deposit functions payable and expecting Ether to be accepted.
  • Not checking msg.sender for privileged operations.
  • Performing state writes without validating conditions first, wasting gas.
Safety patterns
Checks-Effects-Interactions: validate conditions, update state, then interact with external addresses.
Prefer private/internal for helper functions and public/external only for APIs that require broad access.
Test failing paths in Remix to confirm revert behavior and error messages.
Key Takeaway
Apply checks-effects-interactions, be explicit with visibility and payable, and test both success and failure scenarios thoroughly.

screens.title: Live coding plan: from basic to Ownable
screens.narratorSegment: The live-coding plan helps you structure a 15-minute demonstration that grows a basic contract into an Ownable pattern. Start with a minimal contract defining a public state variable and a simple public setter to see default behaviors. Next, explicitly add visibility specifiers to every function and convert setters to external where it improves gas for large data inputs. Then mark read-only functions as view or pure so they can be called off-chain for free. Add deposit payable and verify msg. value handling. Implement the withdraw function with require-based owner checks and safe sequencing. Finally, add a transferOwnership function that only the current owner can call; update the owner variable inside a require-guarded function to change who can perform admin actions. A common misconception is thinking transferOwnership must be public without checks — always require current owner authorization. During the demo, compile and execute each step in Remix, switch accounts to demonstrate reverts, and reflect on when external has a measurable gas benefit for large arrays. This incremental approach shows how visibility and mutability choices evolve as features are added. In practical terms, incrementally add visibility, mutability, and transferownership. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Step sequence

  2. Explicitly add visibility and convert large-parameter setters to external.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize three concise concepts to remember. First, function visibility determines who may call a function: prefer private or internal for helpers, external for calldata-heavy external APIs, and public for general access when needed. Second, state mutability communicates intent and affects costs: pure for computations that don't touch state, view for read-only access, payable when a function must accept Ether, and no specifier for state-changing functions. Third, state variables live on-chain and are expensive to write: validate inputs with require, update storage before external interactions, and restrict access using msg. sender checks to implement owner-only functions. Carry these concepts into every contract you write: choose the narrowest visibility, the most restrictive mutability compatible with your purpose, and guard critical operations with require-based access control. These habits reduce attack surface, make behavior explicit, and help you reason about gas and security.

Mutability

State & Access Control

screens.title: Three reminders before you code
screens.narratorSegment: Before you write or change a contract, keep three quick reminders in mind. One: default to the most restrictive visibility, then widen only when necessary — this reduces accidental exposure. Three: protect sensitive operations with msg. sender checks and require statements, validate preconditions early, update storage before external calls, and test both successful and failing paths in Remix. These reminders are lightweight but powerful: they shape how you structure logic, how expensive your contract is to use, and how resistant it is to simple mistakes. Carry them into your SimpleWallet lab and your next contract. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we will build a clear mental model of Solidity functions, why visibility matters, and how state lives on-chain. Functions are the units of behavior in a smart contract: they accept inputs, produce outputs, and may read or change persistent state. Visibility specifiers — public, private, internal, external — control who can call those functions and are a primary security boundary. State mutability specifiers — view, pure, payable, or none — describe whether a function reads state, only computes, or can accept Ether. State variables, declared outside functions, are stored permanently on the blockchain and are costly to change. Throughout the chapter you'll see concrete code examples, a hands-on SimpleWallet activity, and common mistakes to avoid, like exposing sensitive functions or forgetting payable. By the end you will be able to choose the correct visibility and mutability for a function, manage state variables safely, and implement a basic owner-only access control using msg. sender and require. Notice practical trade-offs: tighter visibility reduces attack surface; pure and view can be called off-chain for free. Keep these ideas in mind as we walk through examples and a live-demo style walkthrough.

By the end of this chapter you will meet four measurable objectives. First, you will be able to define and declare functions in Solidity, including parameters and return values. That means writing correct signatures and returning values where appropriate, and understanding how parameters map to memory locations. Second, you will understand and correctly apply function visibility: public, private, internal, and external, and why choosing the most restrictive visibility reduces attack surface. Third, you will differentiate view, pure, and payable functions, knowing which are free when called off-chain and which accept Ether, and how they affect gas usage. Fourth, you will manage state variables and implement a basic access control mechanism using msg. sender and require so only an owner can run sensitive functions. Each objective includes a short practice milestone: write a utility pure function; convert a setter to external for gas efficiency where appropriate; add payable to a deposit handler; and implement owner-only withdraw logic. These objectives are practical and testable in Remix. Work through the provided SimpleWallet activity to verify each milestone and reflect on a scenario where external is more gas-efficient than public.

This mini-bar guides how you'll move from comprehension to mastery. Learn means you can name and write basic function signatures and state variables. Understand means you can explain the differences between public, private, internal, and external, and state mutability choices. Apply means you will actually implement access control in a contract, mark functions view or pure when appropriate, and test deposit and withdraw behavior in Remix. Master involves choosing the most restrictive visibility by default, minimizing state writes to reduce gas, and reasoning about when external is preferable for array parameters because of calldata efficiency. Each stage contains a concrete practice: write a pure utility, convert a function to external and measure gas on a large array, add payable to a deposit function and observe msg. value, implement require-based owner checks and attempt a failing transaction from a non-owner account. Progress through these steps in the SimpleWallet activity. This structure helps you translate definitions into safe, testable code that you can reason about under adversarial conditions.

A function in Solidity is a named block of code that performs a task, accepts parameters, and can return values. Unlike functions in off-chain languages, Solidity functions also carry metadata: visibility and state mutability specifiers that affect access and gas. When you declare a function you specify its signature — name, parameter types, and return types — and then choose visibility and mutability. For example, a function that only computes and returns a value should be marked pure; one that reads state but doesn't modify it should be view. A function intended to receive Ether must be marked payable. A practical example is a calculateTax function that takes an amount and returns ten percent; it doesn't touch state and should be declared pure so callers can run it off-chain for free. A common misconception is thinking that view or pure always cost no gas; they are free when executed off-chain, but if they are called from another contract in a transaction they still consume gas. Key takeaway: choose the right signature and specifiers to make your intent explicit and your contract safer and cheaper to interact with. Ask yourself: does this function need to modify state or receive Ether? If not, mark it view or pure.

Visibility specifiers control where a function can be called from and are a critical access control layer. Public functions are callable from anywhere: externally, internally, and through inheritance. Private functions are callable only inside the defining contract and cannot be accessed by derived contracts. Internal functions are callable within the contract and by derived contracts, but not by external accounts. External functions can be called from outside the contract; they are often more gas-efficient for large calldata parameters because arguments are read directly from calldata instead of being copied to memory. A concrete example from the source shows a public getter that returns a state value and an external setter that updates it then calls an internal helper. A common pitfall is making administrative logic public by accident; default to the most restrictive visibility and widen only when needed. Another trap is thinking external functions cannot be called internally — they can be, but with different semantics and potential gas implications. Key takeaway: pick the narrowest visibility that still supports your required interactions, and test callability in Remix to validate your assumptions.

State mutability specifiers tell readers and the EVM how a function interacts with blockchain state and Ether. A view function promises not to modify state; it may read state variables and is free when called off-chain. A pure function promises not to read or modify state; it only computes using its inputs and local variables. Payable functions are the only ones that can receive Ether; forgetting to mark a deposit handler payable will revert incoming transfers. Functions with no mutability specifier can both read and write state and will always cost gas when executed on-chain. Consider the deposit and getBalance examples: deposit must be payable to accept msg. value and update balances; getBalance should be view to allow off-chain reads without gas. A common misconception is assuming payable forces a function to process Ether; it only allows Ether to be sent. You still need to inspect msg. value and update state or revert as your logic requires. Key takeaway: choose view/pure to signal and enable free off-chain reads, and use payable only when your function intentionally accepts Ether. State mutability specifiers means mark read-only functions view or pure to reduce cost for callers; mark deposit handlers payable and check msg.value when accepting ether.. In practical terms, view, pure, payable and when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

State variables are declared outside functions and persist in the contract's storage on the blockchain. They are the contract's canonical data and modifying them is the most expensive operation in terms of gas. In practice you should minimize writes, batch updates when possible, and avoid unnecessary writes inside loops. For example, the SimpleWallet contract defines state variables owner and balance; the constructor sets owner using msg. sender and balance is updated in deposit and withdraw functions. Accessing a state variable from a function is straightforward, but remember that reading from storage is cheaper than writing but still costs gas when done within a transaction. A common error is redundantly storing data that can be derived or computed, which inflates gas costs and storage usage. Also be aware of shadowing variables in derived contracts — internal visibility allows inheritance but requires careful naming to avoid accidental overrides. Key takeaway: treat state writes as intentional and costly; design your functions to minimize writes and to validate conditions before changing state, using require to avoid wasted gas on failing operations. State variables and storage means declare persistent data outside functions; minimize writes and validate before modifying storage to avoid wasted gas.. In practical terms, how variables declared outside functions persist on-chain. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through the SimpleWallet starter contract to see these ideas in action. The constructor sets owner to msg. sender at deployment and initializes balance. The deposit function is public and payable; it increments the internal balance by msg. value so the contract tracks deposits explicitly. The getContractBalance function is declared view and returns address(this). balance; this is a read-only operation safe for off-chain calls. The withdraw function is intentionally left with TODOs: it must check that msg. sender equals owner, verify the contract has sufficient balance, perform the transfer, and update the internal balance. When implementing withdraw you should call require(msg. sender == owner, "Only owner can withdraw.") and require(address(this). balance >= _amount, "Insufficient balance.") before transferring funds. A typical mistake is transferring Ether before updating state or failing to guard with require, which can enable unauthorized withdrawals or reentrancy. The guided activity asks you to implement withdraw and test it using different Remix accounts so you observe reverts and successful transfers. Reflect: why should we prefer updating state before external calls to avoid reentrancy? SimpleWallet starter review means complete withdraw with require checks, verify balances, transfer safely, and update internal tracking to avoid vulnerabilities.. In practical terms, constructor, deposit, view getter, and withdraw todos. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Access control is succinctly implemented using msg. sender and require. Msg. sender holds the address initiating the external call. A common owner-only pattern stores owner in a state variable at construction and then checks caller identity with require(msg. sender == owner, "Only owner can...");. The process is straightforward: first, declare owner as a state variable and set it in the constructor using msg. sender. Second, write the sensitive function and at the top enforce the require check. Third, verify preconditions like available balance with another require. Fourth, perform state updates, and finally perform external transfers if needed. Understanding the contrast between view, pure, payable, and normal state-changing functions helps you design efficient and correct contracts. View functions read state but do not modify it; they allow off-chain callers to fetch data without submitting a transaction. Pure functions do not read or modify state and are ideal for utility calculations; both view and pure are free to call off-chain. Payable functions are allowed to receive Ether and must explicitly be marked so, otherwise incoming Ether will cause a revert. Functions without any mutability specifier can change state and therefore always cost gas when executed on-chain. A concrete example: getContractBalance is view and returns address(this). balance; calculateSum is pure and simply returns a sum; deposit is payable and updates state. A common contrast to check is that view and pure do not guarantee zero gas when they are invoked from on-chain context — they still cost gas when called from other contracts. This screen highlights common mistakes you should avoid. First, incorrect visibility: exposing sensitive functions as public instead of private or internal can allow unauthorized actors to change state or drain funds. Second, missing payable: forgetting to mark a deposit handler payable causes incoming Ether to revert, leading to failed transactions and poor UX. Third, unchecked msg. sender: failing to validate caller identity for privileged operations allows unauthorized access; use require(msg. sender == owner, "...") to enforce ownership. Fourth, gas costs of state changes: writes to storage are expensive; design functions to minimize state writes and avoid unnecessary storage updates inside loops. Finally, reentrancy: never transfer Ether and then update state — update state first, then transfer, and consider using checks-effects-interactions pattern. A misconception to clear up is that view and pure always save gas; they are free only off-chain. When called in a transaction from another contract, they still cost gas. The takeaway is to be explicit: choose the most restrictive visibility, mark functions payable only when needed, validate msg. sender, and minimize writes to control gas and attack surface.

Let's summarize three concise concepts to remember. First, function visibility determines who may call a function: prefer private or internal for helpers, external for calldata-heavy external APIs, and public for general access when needed. Second, state mutability communicates intent and affects costs: pure for computations that don't touch state, view for read-only access, payable when a function must accept Ether, and no specifier for state-changing functions. Third, state variables live on-chain and are expensive to write: validate inputs with require, update storage before external interactions, and restrict access using msg. sender checks to implement owner-only functions. Carry these concepts into every contract you write: choose the narrowest visibility, the most restrictive mutability compatible with your purpose, and guard critical operations with require-based access control. These habits reduce attack surface, make behavior explicit, and help you reason about gas and security.

Before you write or change a contract, keep three quick reminders in mind. One: default to the most restrictive visibility, then widen only when necessary — this reduces accidental exposure. Two: mark functions with the correct mutability so readers and the EVM know whether the function is read-only, pure computation, or an Ether receiver; this also helps callers avoid unnecessary gas. Three: protect sensitive operations with msg. sender checks and require statements, validate preconditions early, update storage before external calls, and test both successful and failing paths in Remix. These reminders are lightweight but powerful: they shape how you structure logic, how expensive your contract is to use, and how resistant it is to simple mistakes.
